title: Why the state is in infrastructure at all
blockname: Why the state is in infrastructure at all
notes: Keep this block analytical. The temptation is to describe institutions; the point is to derive them from the failures they exist to correct.
text: Block A Why the state is in infrastructure at all Four market failures, three institutional responses, and the question of which to use when. Indicative length 30 minutes 4

title: The question the week has to answer
blockname: Why the state is in infrastructure at all
notes: Set the question as a puzzle rather than as a preamble. Students find the shipbuilding comparison useful because it separates size from the actual cause.
text: The question the week has to answer Infrastructure is provided almost nowhere by unregulated private markets. Even where assets are privately owned, prices are set by a regulator, entry is licensed, and the state retains a claim on service standards. That is unusual, and it is not explained by the assets being large or expensive: shipbuilding and semiconductor fabrication are both, and neither is regulated this way. The explanation lies in four properties that recur across infrastructure sectors, each of which produces a specific market failure, and each of which has a standard institutional response. The rest of this block derives the institutions from the failures. A 5

title: Four market failures, and what each implies
blockname: Why the state is in infrastructure at all
notes: The last card is the pivot into the rest of the block, and the one the environmental policy students will recognise immediately from EP02.
text: Four market failures, and what each implies Natural monopoly One firm can serve the market more cheaply than two, so competition in the market destroys value. Implies regulation of price and entry, or public ownership. Externalities Costs and benefits fall on parties outside the transaction, so private and social returns diverge. Implies subsidy, taxation, or a planning requirement. Public good characteristics Non-rival and hard to exclude from, so private supply is undersupply. Implies public funding, though not necessarily public provision. Information asymmetry The operator knows its own costs and the regulator does not. Implies incentive regulation rather than cost-plus, and is the reason regulation is hard rather than merely tedious. What they have in common Each is a reason for the state to be involved. None of them says how. Confusing the case for public funding with the case for public provision is the most common error in this field. A Weber, Staub-Bisang and Alfen (2016), ch. 1.3; EP02, fundamental economic concepts I and II. 6

title: Natural monopoly is a claim about costs, not about size
blockname: Why the state is in infrastructure at all
notes: Emphasise that subadditivity is an empirical claim about a specific network at a specific time, not a permanent property. Fibre overbuild in several markets has falsified it for telecoms in dense areas.
text: Natural monopoly is a claim about costs, not about size A natural monopoly exists where the cost function is subadditive over the relevant range, meaning one firm can produce any given output more cheaply than any combination of firms. In network industries this arises because the fixed cost of the network is large and the marginal cost of an additional user is small. Two consequences follow, and they pull in opposite directions. Competition in the market is wasteful, because duplicating the network raises total cost. But a single firm with no competitor and inelastic demand will price above cost. Regulation exists to resolve that tension, and every regulatory instrument in block C is an attempt to obtain the cost advantage without the pricing consequence. A 7

title: Three responses to natural monopoly
blockname: Why the state is in infrastructure at all
notes: Franchise bidding is the intellectual ancestor of the PPP, and its weakness is exactly what block F is about. Competition at the tender is undone by renegotiation after award.
text: Three responses to natural monopoly A Demsetz (1968) is the origin of the franchise bidding argument; Delmon, ch. 1.1.2. 8 Response Mechanism Weakness Where it is used Public ownership The state owns and operates, and sets prices administratively Weak cost discipline; investment competes with other public spending Most road networks; rail infrastructure in many countries Regulation of a private firm Private ownership with a regulator setting allowed revenue and standards Information asymmetry; regulatory capture; risk of underinvestment before a review Water, energy networks and airports in England and Wales Franchise bidding Competition for the market rather than in it, by auctioning the right to serve Contracts are incomplete, so the competition is only as good as the contract Concessions, toll roads, most PPP arrangements

title: The bundling question
blockname: Why the state is in infrastructure at all
notes: Seven pages, and the theoretical spine of the week. If students read one thing, this is it. The teaching move is to ask them to classify a list of services by whether quality is contractible.
text: The bundling question Hart Incomplete contracts and public ownership: remarks, and an application to public-private partnerships, The Economic Journal, 2003. Hart asks when building and operating should be bundled into one contract rather than procured separately. The answer turns on whether quality is contractible. Bundle, and the builder internalises the operating consequences of its design choices, so it builds something cheaper to run. That is the case for the PPP. But the same incentive produces cost cutting wherever quality cannot be specified and enforced, and the operator captures the saving. Bundling is therefore right where the service is measurable, as with a road surface or an available hospital bed, and wrong where it is not, as with the quality of care delivered inside that hospital. A Hart, O. (2003), The Economic Journal 113(486), C69–C76. 9

title: Public private partnerships do not relax the budget constraint
blockname: Why the state is in infrastructure at all
notes: This is the corrective to how ministers talk about PPPs, and it is worth stating with some force. Their further point, that an optimal contract includes a minimum revenue guarantee and a revenue cap, previews block F.
text: Public private partnerships do not relax the budget constraint The most common political justification for a PPP is that it allows investment without public borrowing. Engel, Fischer and Galetovic show that this is an accounting illusion. The state either pays the private partner over the life of the contract, in which case it has borrowed by another name, or it grants the right to charge users, in which case it has given away future revenue it could otherwise have collected. What changes under a PPP is not the budget constraint but the allocation of risk and the incentives on delivery. If a PPP cannot be justified on those grounds, it cannot be justified at all. A Engel, E., Fischer, R. and Galetovic, A. (2013), Journal of the European Economic Association 11(1), 83–111. 10

title: What the state is actually buying
blockname: Why the state is in infrastructure at all
notes: The commitment device argument is the strongest and least discussed. A contracted maintenance obligation survives a spending review; a maintenance line in a departmental budget does not.
text: What the state is actually buying What a PPP can deliver Transfer of construction and completion risk to a party that can price and manage it Whole-life cost discipline, where design and operation sit with one party Delivery capability the public sector does not have in house A commitment device: a contract is harder to raid than a maintenance budget What it cannot deliver Cheaper capital. The state borrows more cheaply than any consortium Escape from the fiscal consequences of the investment Transfer of risks the private party cannot control, such as demand or policy change, at a sensible price Good projects out of bad appraisal. A PPP delivers what was specified A 11

title: Which failure bites, sector by sector
blockname: Why the state is in infrastructure at all
notes: The generation row is the interesting one. Once the natural monopoly was separated out, generation became a competitive market and the remaining failure was the externality, which is now addressed by a price rather than by ownership. That unbundling is the single most successful reform in the sector and worth naming.
text: Which failure bites, sector by sector A 12 Sector Natural monopoly Externality Public good Dominant institutional response Water and sewerage Strong Strong Weak Regulated private or public monopoly Electricity networks Strong Moderate Weak Regulated private monopoly Electricity generation Absent Strong Absent Competitive market with a carbon instrument Roads Strong locally Strong Strong for local roads Public provision, tolling at the margin Rail infrastructure Strong Strong Weak Public or regulated, with franchised operations Fixed telecoms Weakening Moderate Weak Regulated access, with competition where feasible

title: Who exactly is the state
blockname: Why the state is in infrastructure at all
notes: This slide is the antidote to the phrase “the government should”. It also sets up the last card in block G, where the state appears in six roles in a single project.
text: Who exactly is the state Speaking of the state as a single actor obscures the thing that matters. In any real project the public side is several bodies with different objectives: a sponsoring department that wants the asset, a finance ministry that is counting the liability, an economic regulator with a statutory duty to consumers, a consenting authority that must be procedurally fair, a local authority representing people who live nearby, and often a state-owned company that is a commercial party in its own right. Coordination between these is itself an institution, and it is one of the fifteen assessed by PIMA. Where it fails, projects are approved that cannot be funded, or funded that cannot be consented. A IMF PIMA, planning institutions; PGR04 lecture 5, collective action and local governance. 13

title: Externalities have to be priced before they can be weighed
blockname: Why the state is in infrastructure at all
notes: The environmental policy students can lead here. Ask them how a stated preference estimate is produced and how much confidence it deserves, and let the room hear how contestable the numbers in a business case are.
text: Externalities have to be priced before they can be weighed The case for public involvement often rests on effects that fall outside the transaction: emissions, noise, severance, agglomeration, and access for people who could not otherwise reach work. None of these has a market price, and all of them appear in the business case as numbers. Where those numbers come from is a methodological question with a large literature behind it, covering revealed preference, stated preference and benefit transfer, and it is taught in EP02. For this module the important point is narrower: the externality valuations in an appraisal are estimates with wide confidence intervals, and they are frequently the component that determines whether a scheme passes. A EP02, valuing environmental goods and services; PGR02 Michaelmas week 2. 14

title: Block A discussion
blockname: Why the state is in infrastructure at all
notes: Question one takes ten minutes and is the most useful exercise in block A. The prison and the school are the interesting cases because the building is contractible and the service inside it is not.
text: Block A discussion Seminar questions Classify these services by whether quality is contractible, and therefore by whether bundling is appropriate: street lighting, a prison, a school building, teaching in that school, a water treatment works. If the state borrows more cheaply than a consortium, under what conditions can a privately financed project still be the cheaper option overall? Franchise bidding replaces competition in the market with competition for it. What has to be true about the contract for that substitution to work? A 15

title: Public investment management
blockname: Public investment management
notes: No peer university in the comparator set teaches this material as a taught module. The IMF and World Bank frameworks carry it, which means the teaching material here is built rather than borrowed. Take it slowly.
text: Block B Public investment management How a state decides what to build, and the institutions that stop it building the wrong thing. Indicative length 40 minutes 16

title: Selection matters more than volume
blockname: Public investment management
notes: This is the argument for why the block exists. Make it before the machinery, or the machinery looks like administrative detail.
text: Selection matters more than volume Week 1 established that the aggregate return to infrastructure is real but modest, and that the distribution around it is wide. That combination has a direct implication: the value created by an investment programme depends far more on which projects are selected than on how much is spent. Public investment management is the name for the institutions that do the selecting. It is unglamorous, it is where the returns are actually made or lost, and it is almost entirely absent from the finance literature on infrastructure. B 17

title: The public investment management cycle
blockname: Public investment management
notes: Read the failure column aloud. Each failure is observable in a country the students know, and the last one explains why the same errors recur.
text: The public investment management cycle B IMF, Public Investment Management Assessment Handbook, chapters 1 and 2. 18 Stage Question it answers Typical failure Planning What do we need, and does this project belong to a strategy Projects appear from political announcement rather than from a plan Appraisal Do the benefits exceed the costs, under honest assumptions Optimism bias and strategic misrepresentation, as in week 1 Selection Given a budget, which of the appraised projects proceed Selection on political salience rather than on appraised value Budgeting Is the whole-life cost, including maintenance, provided for Capital funded, maintenance not, so the asset degrades Implementation Is it being delivered to time, cost and specification Weak monitoring, and no authority to stop a failing project Evaluation Did it deliver what was claimed, and what do we learn Rarely done, and almost never fed back into appraisal

title: The framework this week uses
blockname: Public investment management
notes: Set an exercise: give each group a country and three institutions from the list, and ask them to score design and effectiveness from public sources. It works well and takes twenty minutes.
text: The framework this week uses 15 Institutions of public investment management assessed by the IMF’s PIMA framework, across planning, allocation and implementation. PIMA is a diagnostic instrument. It scores a country on the design of each institution and on its effectiveness in practice, and the gap between the two is often larger than the gap between countries. Planning institutions cover fiscal rules, national and sectoral plans, coordination between levels of government, and the management of partnerships and of state company investment. Allocation institutions cover multi-year budgeting, budget comprehensiveness and unity, appraisal and selection. Implementation institutions cover funding availability, transparency, project management, asset monitoring and procurement. Its teaching value is that it turns an abstract quality claim into a checklist a student can apply to a real country. B IMF PIMA Handbook, 1st edition, 2022. Institution names should be checked against the current edition. 19

title: The efficiency gap
blockname: Public investment management
notes: Verify this figure before teaching. It is widely cited and I have flagged it because the measurement of public capital stock is genuinely disputed.
text: The efficiency gap About 30% Average gap between the public capital stock a country has and the stock its investment spending should have produced, on IMF estimates. The efficiency gap is calculated by comparing countries on the relationship between cumulative investment spending and the value of the capital stock and services delivered. Countries close to the frontier convert spending into assets efficiently; others do not. The order of magnitude matters more than the precise figure. If roughly a third of public investment spending does not become usable capital, then improving selection and delivery is worth more than any plausible increase in the budget. The estimate is contested and depends heavily on how the capital stock is measured. It is a motivating figure, not a finding to lean on. B IMF, Making Public Investment More Efficient (2015) and subsequent PIMA work. Figure to be verified against the current publication before delivery. 20

title: Norway builds the institution the evidence calls for
blockname: Public investment management
notes: The Norwegian scheme is the working example of what week 1 argued was needed. Its distinctive feature is the concept-stage review, which most gateway systems lack.
text: Norway builds the institution the evidence calls for If cost underestimation is strategic rather than accidental, better forecasting will not fix it and an external check will. Norway operates exactly such a check. Projects above a threshold pass through two mandatory quality assurance stages before funding: the first interrogates the choice of concept, asking whether this is the right problem and the right kind of solution, and the second interrogates cost and management arrangements once a concept is chosen. The reviews are carried out by external consultants under framework agreements with the Ministry of Finance, and they are conducted before political commitment rather than after. The first stage is the more important of the two, because a project that should not exist cannot be rescued by good cost control. B Flyvbjerg (ed.) (2017), The Oxford Handbook of Megaproject Management, ch. 18. Threshold value to be confirmed before delivery. 21

title: The United Kingdom’s version
blockname: Public investment management
notes: Be fair here. The UK system is strong by international standards on appraisal method and weak on the timing of challenge. The planning students will have views.
text: The United Kingdom’s version What exists The Green Book, which sets appraisal method across government, including optimism bias uplifts derived from reference class evidence The Infrastructure and Projects Authority, reviewing major projects and publishing delivery confidence assessments Gateway reviews at defined points in a project’s life The Major Projects Portfolio, which makes the pipeline and its status visible What is weaker than Norway Review generally follows the announcement of a project rather than preceding it The concept stage, asking whether this is the right kind of intervention at all, is less systematically challenged Delivery confidence assessments are advisory, and the authority to stop a project rests elsewhere Evaluation after completion is patchy, so the appraisal evidence base improves slowly B Green Book supplementary guidance on optimism bias; Infrastructure and Projects Authority annual reports. 22

title: Why appraisal fails, and what each remedy actually fixes
blockname: Public investment management
notes: This slide is the bridge to PGR04 for the planning students. Cost underestimation is a rent-seeking equilibrium, not a forecasting failure, and that reframing is the single most useful thing in the block.
text: Why appraisal fails, and what each remedy actually fixes Technical error in forecasting is fixed by better models and better data. This is the least of the problem and the most commonly proposed remedy. Optimism bias, a psychological regularity, is fixed by reference class forecasting: adjust the estimate using the distribution of outcomes for similar projects rather than reasoning from the components of this one. Strategic misrepresentation is not fixed by either, because the promoter knows the true number and has an interest in not stating it. It requires an external check with the authority to stop the project, and accountability for the forecast after the fact. Weak institutions are fixed by none of the above, because the check itself is captured. This is the PIMA argument and the reason institutional quality, not analytical technique, is the binding constraint in many countries. B Flyvbjerg (2014); PGR04 lecture 4, rent-seeking and perverse incentives. 23

title: A pipeline is an institution, not a list
blockname: Public investment management
notes: The last sentence is the analytical point and it connects back to the previous slide.
text: A pipeline is an institution, not a list Investors say repeatedly that the constraint on infrastructure investment in developing markets is not capital but bankable projects. What they mean is that project preparation, which is expensive, slow and frequently wasted, is undersupplied. A credible pipeline does three things at once. It tells investors that a flow of transactions exists, which justifies their building a local capability. It disciplines government by making commitments visible and comparable. And it separates preparation from procurement, so that projects reach the market already appraised. Where preparation is funded only after political commitment, appraisal becomes a justification exercise. B Delmon, ch. 6 and ch. 7; APMG PPP Certification Guide, chapters 3 and 4. 24

title: What a business case contains
blockname: Public investment management
notes: The five case model is the United Kingdom’s standard and versions of it are used internationally. The right-hand column is what an experienced reviewer looks for, and it is worth giving students a real business case to mark against it.
text: What a business case contains B HM Treasury Green Book five case model; PGR02 Michaelmas week 2, the evaluation of urban policy. 25 Case Question Where it is usually weakest Strategic Is there a case for change, and does this fit the strategy Written after the project was chosen, to justify it Economic Does this option maximise public value among the alternatives The options appraised are variants of the preferred option Commercial Is the procurement deliverable, and will the market bid Market appetite assumed rather than tested Financial Is it affordable, in capital and in whole-life terms Capital affordability shown, operating and renewal cost not Management Can the organisation actually deliver it Optimistic about capability, and rarely revisited

title: The discount rate does more work than any other assumption
blockname: Public investment management
notes: Do the arithmetic on the board. It is the clearest demonstration in the module that appraisal is not an objective procedure, and it recurs in week 6 and week 7.
text: The discount rate does more work than any other assumption An infrastructure appraisal compares costs incurred now with benefits accruing for sixty years. The rate at which those future benefits are discounted therefore determines the answer, and it is a value judgement expressed as a number. The United Kingdom uses a social time preference rate built from pure time preference, expected consumption growth and the elasticity of marginal utility, and applies a declining schedule for very long horizons. Small changes matter enormously: at three and a half per cent a benefit sixty years out is worth about an eighth of its face value, and at one and a half per cent about two fifths. Any long-lived asset can be made to pass or fail by a defensible movement in this parameter. B HM Treasury Green Book; EP02, evaluation of environmental policies. 26

title: Optimism bias uplifts, and where they come from
blockname: Public investment management
notes: The fourth bullet is the analytical point and it distinguishes the two failure modes cleanly.
text: Optimism bias uplifts, and where they come from United Kingdom appraisal guidance requires an explicit uplift to capital cost estimates at early stages, calibrated on the historic difference between estimated and outturn cost for comparable projects. This is reference class forecasting embedded in official procedure, and it is the institutional answer to the week 1 evidence. The uplifts are largest for the most novel and least standardised project types, which is where the evidence says they should be. The weakness is that an uplift applied to a deliberately understated base still produces an understated number, so the instrument corrects optimism and not misrepresentation. The other weakness is that uplifts are frequently negotiated down on the grounds that this project is different, which is what every promoter believes. B Green Book supplementary guidance on optimism bias; Flyvbjerg (2002). 27

title: Evaluation is the stage nobody funds
blockname: Public investment management
notes: The final sentence usually lands. The most cited evidence base in the field exists because academics built it, not because states kept records.
text: Evaluation is the stage nobody funds Of the six stages, evaluation after completion is the least performed. The reasons are structural rather than accidental. The team that delivered the project has dispersed, the sponsoring minister has moved on, the counterfactual is hard to construct, and nobody has an interest in a document establishing that the benefits did not appear. The cost of not doing it is that the appraisal evidence base never improves. Reference class forecasting requires a reference class, and a reference class requires that somebody recorded what happened. This is the strongest institutional argument for compulsory post-implementation review, and it is why the Flyvbjerg datasets exist at all: they were assembled by researchers because governments had not assembled them. B PGR02 Michaelmas week 2; EP02, evaluation of environmental policies. 28

title: Block B discussion
blockname: Public investment management
notes: Question three previews block E.
text: Block B discussion Seminar questions Norway reviews the choice of concept before political commitment. What would have to change in the United Kingdom for an equivalent check to bite, and who would resist it? The efficiency gap suggests that a third of public investment does not become usable capital. If you had to improve one of the six stages of the cycle, which would you choose and why? Project preparation is underfunded almost everywhere. Whose job is it to pay for it, and what does the answer imply about the role of development institutions? B 29

title: Economic regulation and the price control
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes:
This is the finance cohort’s foothold in a planning-heavy week. Do the arithmetic on the board. The planning and environmental students will not have seen it and it is the most transferable thing in the block.

The block splits cleanly at the applied case, which runs about twenty-five minutes and can be dropped whole without damaging the theory, or run on its own as the seminar. The case carries the block’s cross-cohort weight: consent regimes and the water stress classification for the planning and environmental students, cost allocation between the asset base and a connecting user for the finance students, and an aggregation problem that belongs to RM01 and therefore to everyone.
text: Block C Economic regulation and the price control What a regulator sets, how it sets it, and why the answer is a weighted average cost of capital. Then an applied case on data centre demand for water and grid capacity. Indicative length 65 minutes 30

title: The regulatory bargain
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: The credibility point is the one to dwell on. A regulator with discretion and no track record cannot attract long-term capital at any allowed return, which is the situation in much of the world.
text: The regulatory bargain Where a network is privately owned and a natural monopoly, the state and the owner strike a bargain. The owner accepts that its prices, service standards and investment obligations are set by an independent regulator. In return the regulator commits to allowing revenue sufficient to finance the efficient operation of the network and to earn a return on the capital invested in it. The bargain is credible only if it survives political pressure, which is why regulators are made independent, and only if the owner believes the return will still be there in fifteen years, which is why regulatory precedent matters more than regulatory rules. C Abor and others (2025), ch. 32. 31

title: The building blocks of an allowed revenue
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: Write the identity on the board: allowed revenue equals the asset base multiplied by the cost of capital, plus depreciation, plus efficient operating cost, plus or minus incentives. Everything in a price review is an argument about one of those four terms.
text: The building blocks of an allowed revenue C RE01 session 3, capital structure and the weighted average cost of capital. 32 Component What it covers Where the argument is Return on the regulatory asset base The cost of the capital tied up in the network The weighted average cost of capital, and what counts as being in the asset base Return of capital, or depreciation Recovery of the investment over the asset’s life Asset lives, which determine how quickly customers pay for an asset Operating expenditure allowance Efficient running costs for the period What is efficient, benchmarked against comparable firms Incentive adjustments Rewards and penalties against output targets Whether the targets were demanding, and whether outperformance is skill or forecast error

title: The allowed return is a weighted average cost of capital
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: Ask the finance students what happens to a company’s share price when the regulator’s draft determination moves the allowed return. The answer, that it moves immediately and sharply, makes the point that regulatory risk is priced.
text: The allowed return is a weighted average cost of capital The single most consequential number in a price control is the allowed return, and it is a weighted average cost of capital calculated by a regulator rather than by a company. Gearing, the cost of debt, the risk-free rate, the equity risk premium and the beta all appear, and each is contested at every review, because a difference of fifty basis points on a large asset base is worth a great deal of money. For students who have taken RE01 this is a familiar calculation in an unfamiliar setting. The unfamiliar part is that the number is not discovered in a market: it is determined administratively, published, and then defended in front of an appeal body. C RE01 session 3. 33

title: Two regulatory regimes
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: The Averch and Johnson distortion is the reason asset base regulation attracts capital. It is also why regulated utilities are accused of gold-plating, and why regulators scrutinise capital expenditure so heavily.
text: Two regulatory regimes Rate of return regulation The firm recovers its costs plus an allowed return on its asset base Low risk for the firm, and low incentive to reduce cost The Averch and Johnson result: a regulated firm over-invests in capital relative to the efficient mix, because the return is earned on the asset base Historically dominant in the United States Incentive regulation Prices are capped for a period, and the firm keeps what it saves within it Strong cost incentive within a period, and a ratchet problem across periods Requires the regulator to forecast efficient cost, which is where the information asymmetry bites The RPI minus X framework, developed in the United Kingdom and now widespread C Averch, H. and Johnson, L. (1962); Littlechild (1983) on RPI minus X. 34

title: The regulator’s problem in one sentence
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: For the environmental policy students this is the moment the block becomes familiar. The regulator and the environmental regulator face the identical problem and use the identical instruments.
text: The regulator’s problem in one sentence The regulator must set an allowance for costs it cannot observe, on the basis of information supplied by the party whose payment depends on that information. The standard responses are benchmarking against comparable firms, menus that make it profitable to reveal a true cost forecast, and outcome-based targets that avoid specifying inputs at all. Each response is a mechanism design solution to an adverse selection problem, which is the EP02 material applied to a network utility rather than to a polluter. None of them removes the asymmetry. They shift how much of the resulting rent the firm retains. C EP02, environmental policy under asymmetric information. 35

title: What can go wrong with a regulator
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: The hold-up in reverse card is the important one for this course. It explains why regulatory precedent has a value that no legal drafting can substitute for.
text: What can go wrong with a regulator Capture The regulator comes to share the industry’s view of what is reasonable, through information dependence and career flows in both directions. Political interference Prices are salient. A government facing an election has an interest in the outcome of a price review and often has instruments to influence it. Hold-up in reverse Once the capital is sunk, the state can allow a lower return than was implied when the investment was made. Rational investors anticipate this and demand more. Ratchet effects A firm that reveals what efficiency is achievable is given a harder target next time, so it does not reveal it. Complexity A regime with enough special provisions becomes unintelligible to anyone outside it, which weakens accountability and favours incumbents. Underinvestment Where the allowed return is set below the true cost of capital, the firm invests less than the regime intends and quality falls with a long lag. C 36

title: A case worth carrying through the module
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: A good group project candidate, and one where public documentation is unusually complete. Ofwat publishes the determinations, the companies publish their responses, and the appeals are on the record.
text: A case worth carrying through the module The water and sewerage industry in England and Wales is the most studied regulated network in the world, and every element of this block is visible in it: a privatised natural monopoly, a regulatory asset base, five-yearly price reviews, an allowed return that is publicly argued over, comparative benchmarking across companies, incentive mechanisms on leakage and pollution, an appeal route to the competition authority, and a political environment that has become hostile. It is also a case where the financial structures adopted by owners, including high gearing and complex holding company arrangements, have become the subject of the regulatory argument rather than a private matter. That makes it the right case for a course about investment as well as regulation. C 37

title: The regulatory asset base is the thing investors actually buy
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: This slide is the one the finance students will take away. It also explains, without any moralising, why regulated utilities have been accused of building things they did not need.
text: The regulatory asset base is the thing investors actually buy A regulated network company is, financially, a claim on a regulatory asset base. Capital expenditure approved by the regulator is added to the base, depreciation removes it, and inflation indexation raises it. The company earns the allowed return on whatever the base is, so the investment case reduces to two questions: how fast will the base grow, and what return will be allowed on it. This has a consequence students find counter-intuitive. A regulated utility is rewarded for investing, because investment enlarges the base on which it earns. Where the regulator is a weak scrutineer of capital expenditure, that is the Averch and Johnson distortion in operation, and it is why capital plans are examined so much more aggressively than operating costs. C RE01 session 3; Abor ch. 32. 38

title: How modern price controls have changed
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: Menu regulation is a direct application of mechanism design and is the clearest example in the course of theory changing practice. It is worth five minutes for the environmental policy students, who will recognise the structure.
text: How modern price controls have changed Total expenditure rather than separate capital and operating allowances, which removes the incentive to classify spending as capital in order to earn a return on it. Outcome-based targets specified as what customers experience, rather than as inputs the company must buy. Menu regulation, in which a company chooses from a schedule of forecast and incentive combinations, and the choice reveals its private cost estimate. Comparative benchmarking across companies, which substitutes for the information the regulator does not have. Longer control periods, which strengthen the within-period incentive and worsen the forecasting problem. C EP02, environmental policy under asymmetric information. 39

title: Airport regulation, and why it matters for the guest session
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: This is the bridge from block C to block G, and it is the question in the guest list that a practitioner can answer far better than an academic.
text: Airport regulation, and why it matters for the guest session A designated United Kingdom airport is regulated by the Civil Aviation Authority, which sets a cap on charges to airlines using the same building blocks as any other price control: an asset base, an allowed return, forecast passenger volumes and efficiency targets. The regulated entity is privately owned and its investment case depends on the determination. The relevance to Heathrow expansion is direct. Consent and regulation are separate processes on separate timetables with separate decision-makers, and a promoter needs both. A consent without a determination that permits recovery of the cost is worth nothing, and a determination cannot sensibly be made before the scheme is defined. Managing that sequencing is one of the hardest practical problems in the case. C Civil Aviation Authority price control determinations. Current regime detail to be confirmed before delivery. 40

title: An applied case, and what it is a case of
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: Set this up as a puzzle rather than a conclusion. Tell them you are going to show two charts that settle an argument, and then show that the charts settle the wrong argument. The pivot is the teaching point and it lands better if they have first accepted the aggregate.
text: An applied case, and what it is a case of The rest of this block works a single live example: the demand that data centres place on water and on grid capacity. It is placed here because the question it ends on, which is who pays when one user requires the network to be reinforced, is a price control question and belongs with the material above. The case is not really about data centres. It is about a measurement problem that recurs across every sector in this module. A national aggregate can be honestly compiled, correctly reported, and still answer a question nobody was asking, because infrastructure demand does not arrive as a share of a national total. It arrives as a point load on one local system. C Full case material, with sources and verification, in the Reality Check folder under Resources. 41

title: Water use in England by category, 2024/25
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: The number to say aloud: data centres take about 5 million litres a day, against 2.6 billion litres a day lost to leaks. That is a ratio of roughly one to five hundred. The log axis is mine, not the broadcast’s; say so, because the choice of axis is itself part of the lesson.
text: Water use in England by category, 2024/25 Public argument about data centres has focused on water. This is the whole English picture for 2024/25, on a logarithmic scale because on a linear one the data centre bar cannot be seen at all. C Environment Agency, Water resources 2024 to 2025; WRc and MOSL, Water-Efficient Data Centres, February 2026. 42

title: Distribution input and leakage in England, 2005 to 2024
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: Ask what has to be true for a sector to be invisible on this chart. Then ask whether invisibility at national scale tells you anything about the town where the facility is actually built. That question is the hinge into the next slide.
text: Distribution input and leakage in England, 2005 to 2024 The same conclusion over twenty years. Total water put into supply has been flat, leakage has barely moved, and data centre use is too small to form a visible band. C Environment Agency, Water Resource Management Plan annual review data. 43

title: What question do those two charts answer?
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: Most of the room will accept the aggregate as decisive on first showing. Let them, then run question two. The answer is that the charts refute a national claim nobody made and are silent on the local claim that was actually being advanced. Do not supply this; wait for a student to reach it.
text: What question do those two charts answer? Seminar questions State the question the charts answer precisely, in one sentence, before deciding whether it is the right question. A campaigner objects to a specific data centre on water grounds. Do these charts refute that objection? What would you need to measure instead, and at what geography, for the objection to be tested rather than dismissed? C 44

title: Data centre locations against water stress classification
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: This reverses the conclusion the charts invited without contradicting a single number in them. Both are true. The aggregate is small and the concentration is extreme, and it is the concentration that determines whether any particular scheme is feasible.
text: Data centre locations against water stress classification The same evidence, disaggregated. Areas shaded dark are those the Environment Agency classified in 2021 as seriously water stressed. The points are the data centres recorded in OpenStreetMap. Nothing here contradicts a number on the previous two slides. The national total really is small. It is simply that the national total was never the quantity that determined whether any particular scheme could be built. What a water company faces is not a share of a national aggregate but a specific abstraction request, in a specific catchment, in a specific dry year. C Environment Agency water stressed areas classification, 2021; facility locations from OpenStreetMap. 45

title: The concentration the aggregate concealed
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: Say the denominator out loud. A student who repeats this figure in an essay without it has learned the wrong lesson from a slide about measurement.
text: The concentration the aggregate concealed 83 per cent of data centres in England and Wales sit in seriously water stressed areas Of the 269 facilities OpenStreetMap records in England and Wales, 224 fall inside water company areas the Environment Agency classified as seriously water stressed in 2021. Against the full United Kingdom count of 288 the share is 78 per cent. The classification does not extend to Scotland or Northern Ireland, which is why the smaller denominator is the meaningful one, and why it should be stated whenever the figure is used. C Author’s calculation. OpenStreetMap is crowd-sourced and incomplete: adequate to show a pattern, inadequate to count. 46

title: Within the sector, the same problem again
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: The fractal point: aggregation misleads at national level, and it misleads again inside the sector. A mean is the wrong statistic for any quantity distributed like this, which is a research methods point as much as a policy one and worth naming as RM01 material.
text: Within the sector, the same problem again C WRc and MOSL, Water-Efficient Data Centres, February 2026. Sample of 257 English facilities. 47 Measure Value What it implies English data centres using under 1,000 m³ a year 67 per cent, mean 217 m³ Most facilities use about as much water as a 600 m² office Share of sector water use taken by the largest six 65 per cent Sector water use is a handful of sites, not a distribution around a mean Share taken by the largest fifteen over 80 per cent A sector average is close to meaningless as a planning input Of those six largest, in service since 2020 five, two of them in 2024 The concentration is recent and still moving

title: A quantity that is metered, billed, and still disputed
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: Worth dwelling on for a course about how assets are appraised and financed. A basic operating quantity cannot be established from the public record. That is a more useful illustration of data risk than any general exhortation about data quality.
text: A quantity that is metered, billed, and still disputed Five-fold the gap between two credible published estimates of the same figure WRc and MOSL put English data centre water use at 1,879,000 m³ a year. Foxglove and The Times reported water companies supplying almost 10 billion litres a year to 231 facilities. The quantity is metered at the point of supply and invoiced monthly, so the discrepancy is not a measurement difficulty. Nobody is obliged to report it, which is why the report’s central recommendation is a mandatory reporting framework. C WRc and MOSL, Water-Efficient Data Centres, February 2026. 48

title: The grid position, which is the binding constraint
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: Preserve the caveat the source itself makes: much of this is speculative and many projects will never be built. A connection queue is an option register, not a demand forecast, and the whole seminar question below turns on that distinction.
text: The grid position, which is the binding constraint C Ofgem and National Energy System Operator figures as reported. Connection register, not a build programme. 49 Quantity Figure What it is, and is not Data centre projects seeking connection, per Ofgem around 140, roughly 50 GW Projects that have applied, not projects that will be built All large-user applications, end July 125 GW, up from 41 GW under a year earlier An application register, tripling in under a year Data centre share of that total at least 80 GW Larger than the whole system at peak British peak electricity demand, 2023 58 GW The system the queue is queuing for

title: Non-domestic electricity demand per square kilometre
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: Read alongside the water map: the two constraints concentrate in the same places, which is not a coincidence. Both follow fibre routes, land availability and proximity to demand, so a site that is hard to supply with water is often hard to connect as well.
text: Non-domestic electricity demand per square kilometre The same concentration, seen from the electricity side. Density rather than total, because density is what a distribution network actually has to carry. A large authority with moderate demand poses no problem; a small one with concentrated demand does. The top thirty of 350 British local authorities take 26.5 per cent of all non-domestic consumption. Slough, singled out in the case, draws 1,786 GWh across about 32 square kilometres. Fifty-seven per cent of the mapped facilities fall inside the inset alone. C DESNZ sub-national electricity consumption, 2024. Inset covers London and the Thames Valley. 50

title: A connection queue is a free option on scarce capacity
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: Question one is the analytical core and takes five minutes. Questions three and four are where the finance content of the week reattaches, and they connect straight back to the allowed revenue identity: reinforcement funded through the asset base earns a return and is recovered from customers over decades. There is no settled British answer, so leave it open rather than resolving it.
text: A connection queue is a free option on scarce capacity Seminar questions If applying to connect is cheap and refundable, what will the size of the queue tell you about real demand? Why is over-subscription the expected outcome rather than a surprise? Three ways to ration scarce capacity: price the option, allocate by queue position, or allocate by readiness to build. Take one each and argue it, including who it disadvantages. A single hyperscale user requires network reinforcement. Who should pay, the user or the regulated asset base and therefore every bill payer? Does the answer change if the facility is designated critical national infrastructure? American operators have signed a pledge to fund their own connection infrastructure rather than socialise it. Would you expect that commitment to survive a downturn, and what would make it credible? C 51

title: Block C discussion
blockname: Economic regulation and the price control
notes: Question three is the one that connects back to week 1, block D. Regulated infrastructure is often described as low risk; what has actually happened is that the risk has changed type.
text: Block C discussion Seminar questions A regulator lowers the allowed return by fifty basis points. Trace the consequences for the company’s share price, its investment programme, and its customers over the following ten years. Incentive regulation gives strong cost discipline within a period and creates a ratchet across periods. How would you design a regime that mitigates the ratchet without abandoning the incentive? Is the risk that a regulated network faces genuinely lower than that of an unregulated firm, or has it merely been converted from market risk into political risk? C 52

title: Delivery models and the PPP framework
blockname: Delivery models and the PPP framework
notes: Delmon Part II is the source for most of this. Keep the emphasis on the framework rather than on the contract, which is week 4.
text: Block D Delivery models and the PPP framework What the state is contracting for, the cycle it runs to get there, and the framework that has to exist first. Indicative length 40 minutes 53

title: The delivery spectrum, with what transfers
blockname: Delivery models and the PPP framework
notes: The two columns that matter are demand risk and end ownership. Every other difference follows from those two choices.
text: The delivery spectrum, with what transfers D Delmon, ch. 1.1.2; Weber ch. 3.1 and 3.2. 54 Model Who designs and builds Who operates Who bears demand risk Who owns at the end Traditional procurement Contractor, to the state’s design The state The state The state throughout Design and build Contractor, to an output specification The state The state The state throughout Availability PPP Consortium Consortium The state Transfers to the state on expiry Concession Consortium Consortium The concessionaire Transfers to the state on expiry Privatisation with regulation The owner The owner Shared through the price control The owner, indefinitely

title: The label is not the transaction
blockname: Delivery models and the PPP framework
notes: Give students a short description of three real transactions with the labels removed and ask them to answer the four questions. It works better than any taxonomy slide.
text: The label is not the transaction The vocabulary in this field is unreliable. The same structure is called a PPP in one country, a concession in another and a private finance initiative in a third, and identical labels describe materially different risk allocations. Delmon’s advice is to ignore the label and read the risk allocation, and it is sound. Four questions identify any structure. Who is paid, and by whom. What triggers the payment: use of the asset, or its availability. What happens if the asset is not available. And what happens at expiry. Answer those and the label is irrelevant. D Delmon, ch. 1.1.1 and 1.1.3. 55

title: The PPP project cycle
blockname: Delivery models and the PPP framework
notes: The implementation row is the one that gets least attention and causes most of the trouble. A twenty-five year contract managed by two people who change every three years is the norm, not the exception.
text: The PPP project cycle D Delmon, ch. 1.5 and ch. 7 to ch. 9; APMG PPP Certification Guide, chapters 3 to 5. 56 Stage What happens Where it goes wrong Selection and prioritisation The project is identified, screened against a plan, and tested for PPP suitability Projects selected because they can be financed off balance sheet rather than because they should be Development Feasibility, business case, market sounding, structuring, advisers appointed Preparation underfunded, so the project reaches the market half formed Procurement and award Prequalification, bidding, evaluation, negotiation, financial close Too few bidders; changes during negotiation that undo the competition Implementation Construction, commissioning, operation, contract management, handback Contract management resourced far below what the contract requires

title: What a PPP framework has to contain
blockname: Delivery models and the PPP framework
notes: Delmon’s Part II is the best treatment in the set texts and this slide is its summary. The lenders’ perspective on the legal list is week 4 material.
text: What a PPP framework has to contain Legal framework Authority for the contracting agency to enter the transaction at all Ability to give the assurances lenders require, including on termination compensation Procurement rules that permit the process the transaction needs Land acquisition powers, and a route to secure title Enforceable security over assets and revenues, and a workable dispute resolution route Institutional framework A unit with responsibility for the programme and the capacity to run it Approval gateways with genuine authority to stop a transaction Fiscal risk management, so contingent liabilities are recorded and priced A project team that survives the transition from procurement to operation Monitoring and evaluation that feeds back into the next transaction D Delmon, ch. 4 and ch. 5. 57

title: PPP units and where they sit
blockname: Delivery models and the PPP framework
notes: The promoter and gatekeeper conflict is the same conflict as in the appraisal discussion in block B, and worth naming as such.
text: PPP units and where they sit Most countries running a PPP programme create a dedicated unit. Where it sits determines what it can do. A unit inside the finance ministry can enforce fiscal discipline and refuse transactions, but is often distrusted by line ministries and can become a bottleneck. A unit inside a line ministry has sector knowledge and a promotional interest, which is exactly the conflict the gateway is supposed to prevent. A unit outside government as an agency has independence and usually lacks authority. The design question is whether the unit is a promoter or a gatekeeper. Asking it to be both, which is common, produces a body that approves its own transactions. D Delmon, ch. 5.3; IMF PIMA institution 4, public private partnerships. 58

title: Fiscal risk is the part that is usually missed
blockname: Delivery models and the PPP framework
notes: This connects the block back to Engel, Fischer and Galetovic in block A. The illusion is only sustainable while the liabilities are invisible.
text: Fiscal risk is the part that is usually missed A PPP creates future obligations for the state: availability payments, minimum revenue guarantees, termination compensation, and exposure to events specified in the contract. Where these are not recorded, priced and reported alongside conventional debt, a government can accumulate a liability it does not know the size of. The consequence is not hypothetical. Several countries have discovered guarantee exposures that materially changed their fiscal position, and the discovery generally coincided with the event that triggered them. Recording contingent liabilities is therefore not an accounting nicety but the mechanism that stops the off-balance-sheet motive from driving project selection. D Delmon, ch. 5.2 and ch. 10.5; IMF PIMA implementation institutions. 59

title: The evaluation evidence is contradictory
blockname: Delivery models and the PPP framework
notes: Resist the temptation to resolve this. The contested state of the evidence is itself the finding, and it is why the module teaches the mechanism rather than the verdict.
text: The evaluation evidence is contradictory Contested Hodge and Greve’s verdict after reviewing the international performance evidence on public private partnerships. The honest position on PPP performance is that the evidence does not settle it. Studies differ on the counterfactual, on whether transaction costs are counted, on whether the comparison is with the public sector as it actually performs or as it is assumed to perform, and on whose account of risk transfer is accepted. Hodge and Greve add a governance argument that is independent of the value for money question. Long-term contracts move decisions out of the political arena for decades, which is a benefit if you think politics is the problem and a cost if you think accountability matters. Students should leave able to state the case on both sides rather than holding a position they cannot defend. D Hodge, G. A. and Greve, C. (2007), Public Administration Review 67(3), 545–558. 60

title: Measuring how supportive a framework is
blockname: Delivery models and the PPP framework
notes: A good coursework exercise: apply the index to a country not in the original sample and defend the scores.
text: Measuring how supportive a framework is Verhoest and colleagues build a governmental support index across twenty European countries, scoring the extent to which the national institutional framework is conducive to public private partnerships. The instrument covers policy and political commitment, the legal and regulatory environment, the presence and role of dedicated units, and practical support for procuring authorities. For a comparative exercise this is more useful than a narrative, because it forces the analyst to say what an institutional framework consists of and to score each element. The planning students will recognise the method from the typologies of national planning systems in PGR01. D Verhoest, K., Petersen, O. H., Scherrer, W. and Soecipto, R. M. (2015), Transport Reviews 35(2), 118–139; PGR01 Michaelmas lecture 2. 61

title: Value for money and the public sector comparator
blockname: Delivery models and the PPP framework
notes: Ask the students what would make a public sector comparator credible. The answer they converge on, that it must be produced by somebody with no interest in the outcome, is the same institutional answer as in block B.
text: Value for money and the public sector comparator The standard test asks whether a privately financed option delivers better value than conventional procurement. It is operationalised by building a public sector comparator: a costing of the same output delivered publicly, adjusted for the risks the public sector would retain. The method is defensible in principle and fragile in practice, because the answer is determined by the risk adjustment, and the risk adjustment is an assumption. Where the comparator is constructed after a policy preference has been formed, it tends to confirm it. The most useful discipline is to require that the risk adjustment be stated as a probability distribution over specific events rather than as a single percentage. D Delmon, ch. 1.2; APMG PPP Certification Guide, chapter 3. 62

title: Unsolicited proposals
blockname: Delivery models and the PPP framework
notes: Worth including because it is common in the emerging markets many students will work in, and because it is a live issue in data centre and renewable development in several countries.
text: Unsolicited proposals A private party approaches government with a project nobody asked for. The attraction is genuine: the proponent may have identified something the state had not, and may bring a technology or a site nobody else has. The difficulty is that there is no competition, no comparison and no market price, and the state is negotiating with the only party that has done the work. The usual responses are to run a competitive process after the fact with a bonus or right to match for the originator, or to buy the intellectual property and tender the project properly. Both are imperfect, and countries that have accepted unsolicited proposals at scale have generally regretted it. D Delmon, ch. 8.5. 63

title: Contract management after financial close
blockname: Delivery models and the PPP framework
notes: This slide covers the twenty-five years that get about five per cent of the attention. It is also where a student going into practice will actually spend their time.
text: Contract management after financial close A twenty-five year contract requires an active counterparty for twenty-five years. In practice the public side is usually resourced for the procurement and not for the operation. The transition itself is the risk point: the team that negotiated the contract disperses, and the people who inherit it did not write it and often cannot find the schedules. Payment mechanisms have to be operated, deductions applied, and performance monitored. A deduction never applied is a term that does not exist. Changes are inevitable over a long contract, and each one is a bilateral negotiation with a party that knows the state cannot walk away. Handback at expiry, with the asset in a specified condition, is planned for far too late where it is planned for at all. D Delmon, ch. 9. 64

title: Block D discussion
blockname: Delivery models and the PPP framework
text: Block D discussion Seminar questions A minister wants a hospital delivered as a PPP because the capital cost will not score against the borrowing target. What should the finance ministry say, and what institution should have prevented the question from arising? Should a PPP unit be a promoter or a gatekeeper? If it cannot be both, which function should sit with the unit and where should the other go? The performance evidence on PPPs is contradictory. What study design would actually settle the question, and why has nobody run it? D 65

title: Development institutions and the multilateral layer
blockname: Development institutions and the multilateral layer
notes: Short block. It sets up the IFC guest in week 4 and the mobilisation material in week 3.
text: Block E Development institutions and the multilateral layer Who lends where commercial capital will not, and what they supply beyond money. Indicative length 25 minutes 66

title: The institutional layer
blockname: Development institutions and the multilateral layer
notes: The last card is the one to insist on. A development institution is optimising something other than return, and students who forget that misread every decision it makes.
text: The institutional layer Multilateral development banks Owned by member states, lending to sovereigns and to the private sector. The World Bank Group, the regional banks, and newer entrants such as the AIIB and the New Development Bank. Development finance institutions Investing in private projects with a development mandate. The IFC, and bilateral institutions such as British International Investment and DEG. Export credit agencies Supporting exports from their home country through direct lending, guarantees and insurance. Often the only source of long tenor debt in difficult jurisdictions. Bilateral aid agencies Grant and concessional funding, frequently for project preparation, which is the stage the market does not fund. Climate funds Concessional capital targeted at mitigation and adaptation, with their own eligibility rules and appraisal processes. What they share A mandate that is not a required return, which explains behaviour that looks irrational to a commercial investor and is not. E Abor and others (2025), ch. 16; Gatti, ch. 6.4 and 6.5. 67

title: What they supply beyond capital
blockname: Development institutions and the multilateral layer
notes: The standards point is the one that surprises students. A development bank in a syndicate is a regulator that has bought its way to the table.
text: What they supply beyond capital Tenor. Commercial lenders will not lend for twenty years in most emerging markets; a development institution will, and its participation lengthens what others will offer. Political risk absorption. Their presence in a syndicate changes the calculus of expropriation and of contract breach, which is the empirical finding in Hainz and Kleimeier. Preferred creditor treatment. Sovereigns have historically serviced multilateral debt through crises, which lowers expected loss for everyone in the structure. Standards. Environmental and social requirements propagate through the syndicate and into the project documents, which is regulation by lending. Preparation. Feasibility work, transaction advice and capacity building, which is undersupplied because it is expensive and often wasted. E Hainz, C. and Kleimeier, S. (2012), Journal of Financial Intermediation 21(2), 287–314. 68

title: The mobilisation claim
blockname: Development institutions and the multilateral layer
notes: The final paragraph is the balanced position. The effect is real and it is an order of magnitude smaller than the gap narrative requires.
text: The mobilisation claim 7 to 1 Bank credit crowded in per dollar of multilateral lending over a three-year period, on syndicated loan data for developing countries between 1993 and 2017. Broccolini and colleagues estimate mobilisation effects directly rather than by assertion. Multilateral participation raises the size of bank inflows, the number of lenders, and the average maturity of syndicated loans, and the effects persist for up to three years without being offset by a decline in bond financing. The result matters because the entire blended finance agenda rests on the claim that concessional capital brings commercial capital with it. Until this paper the claim was largely institutional self-reporting. It is also a ceiling on expectations. Seven to one is a good multiplier and it is not the hundred-to-one implied by some official rhetoric about closing the investment gap. E Broccolini, C., Lotti, G., Maffioli, A., Presbitero, A. F. and Stucchi, R. (2021), The World Bank Economic Review 35(2), 521–543. 69

title: Preferred creditor treatment, and what sustains it
blockname: Development institutions and the multilateral layer
notes: The mechanism is reputational and self-enforcing rather than legal, which makes it a good example of an institution that exists without a rule behind it.
text: Preferred creditor treatment, and what sustains it Sovereign borrowers have historically continued to service multilateral debt through crises in which they defaulted on commercial obligations. Nothing in law requires this. It is sustained because a country that defaults on a multilateral loses access to the institution that lends counter-cyclically, precisely when it most needs one. For a project this matters directly. A development bank in the lending group lowers expected loss for everyone in the structure, which is why its participation changes pricing and tenor for the commercial lenders alongside it rather than only for its own tranche. It is also why the treatment is guarded so carefully by the institutions that benefit from it. E Gatti, ch. 6.4. 70

title: Blended finance, and the risk in it
blockname: Development institutions and the multilateral layer
notes: The additionality framing is the bridge to the planning students, who will have met exactly this question in the evaluation of urban policy.
text: Blended finance, and the risk in it Blended finance uses concessional public capital to make a transaction viable for commercial investors: a first-loss tranche, a guarantee, an interest subsidy, or grant funding for preparation. The intention is to move a project from unbankable to bankable and to bring in capital that would not otherwise arrive. Two risks follow. The first is that the concession is larger than needed, so public money subsidises a return that would have been earned anyway. The second is adverse selection: the projects that need blending most are the ones commercial investors judged worst, and there is a reason for that judgement. The discipline is to ask what would have happened without the concessional element, which is the same additionality question the evaluation literature asks. E Broccolini and others (2021); PGR02 Michaelmas week 2, on additionality. 71

title: Block E discussion
blockname: Development institutions and the multilateral layer
text: Block E discussion Seminar questions If a development institution lends at below the commercial rate, is it subsidising the project, the sponsor, or the commercial lenders alongside it? Preferred creditor treatment is a convention rather than a legal right. What sustains it, and what would happen if it broke? Project preparation is a public good for the market as a whole. Who should fund it, and does the answer differ between a middle income and a low income country? E 72

title: Contracts that do not hold
blockname: Contracts that do not hold
notes: This block is where franchise bidding from block A comes back and fails. It is short, empirical and satisfying to teach.
text: Block F Contracts that do not hold Renegotiation, its causes, and what it does to the competition that preceded it. Indicative length 30 minutes 73

title: The problem franchise bidding was supposed to solve
blockname: Contracts that do not hold
notes: State the logic first, then give the evidence. The reversal lands better that way.
text: The problem franchise bidding was supposed to solve Competition for the market replaces competition in it: bidders compete at tender, and the winner is the one offering the lowest tariff or the highest payment. If the competition is genuine, the monopoly rent is competed away at the moment of award. The argument holds only if the contract that is awarded is the contract that is performed. Where terms are renegotiated afterwards, the competition selected the bidder most willing to bid aggressively and renegotiate later, which is close to the opposite of what was intended. F Demsetz (1968); Guasch, Laffont and Straub (2008). 74

title: How often concessions are renegotiated
blockname: Contracts that do not hold
notes: Verify the exact renegotiation percentages before teaching. The dataset size and period are confirmed; I have not confirmed the sector shares.
text: How often concessions are renegotiated Frequently Guasch, Laffont and Straub analyse close to one thousand concessions awarded in Latin America and the Caribbean between 1989 and 2000, across telecommunications, energy, transport and water. Renegotiation in their data is common rather than exceptional, and markedly more common in water and transport than in telecommunications and energy. It typically occurs within the first few years of a contract intended to run for decades. Their model treats renegotiation as the consequence of imperfect enforcement, and tests what raises its probability. Regulatory institutions matter, contract design matters, and economic shocks matter, but so do features of the award itself. The sector pattern is informative. Where technology changes quickly and competition is possible, contracts hold less well in theory and better in practice; where the asset is a genuine monopoly serving households, renegotiation is close to routine. F Guasch, J. L., Laffont, J.-J. and Straub, S. (2008), International Journal of Industrial Organization 26(2), 421–442. Sector renegotiation rates to be verified against the paper before delivery. 75

title: What raises the probability of renegotiation
blockname: Contracts that do not hold
notes: The second item is the actionable one. Awarding on price alone with no test of deliverability produces the winner’s curse and then the renegotiation.
text: What raises the probability of renegotiation The absence of a regulator at the time of award, or a regulator without the independence to refuse. Award on the basis of the lowest tariff without qualification, which rewards aggressive bidding. Investment obligations specified in inputs rather than outputs, which invites argument about whether they were met. A price cap regime rather than rate of return, which places more risk on the concessionaire and therefore more pressure at the point of shock. Corruption and weak legal enforcement, both of which lower the cost of asking. Macroeconomic shocks, which supply the occasion even where they are not the cause. F Guasch, Laffont and Straub (2008). 76

title: Hold-up, and why sunk capital changes everything
blockname: Contracts that do not hold
notes: Williamson’s fundamental transformation is the underlying idea. It is worth naming even though it is not on the reading list, because it explains the entire contractual architecture of week 4.
text: Hold-up, and why sunk capital changes everything Before the investment is made, the state faces a competitive market of potential concessionaires. After it is made, it faces one party whose capital cannot be moved. The relationship has been transformed from a competitive one into a bilateral monopoly, and both sides now have an incentive to reopen terms. The state can lower the allowed tariff, knowing the asset will keep operating. The concessionaire can threaten to stop serving customers who vote. Neither threat is credible in isolation and both are used. Every device in a concession agreement, from termination compensation to step-in rights to dispute resolution, exists to manage the consequences of this transformation. F Hart (2003); Delmon, ch. 15 and ch. 18. 77

title: Designing against renegotiation
blockname: Contracts that do not hold
notes: The last item on the right is the practical lesson. A bid well below the pack is not a bargain; it is a renegotiation with a delay built in.
text: Designing against renegotiation What helps An independent regulator in place before award, not created afterwards Award criteria that test deliverability as well as price Output specifications, which are harder to argue about than inputs Explicit and pre-agreed rules for the events most likely to trigger a request, including inflation, exchange rate movement and change in law Transparency, so that a renegotiation is publicly visible What does not help Longer contracts, which increase the range of events not provided for More detailed specification, beyond the point where detail can be monitored Penalties that the state will not impose because the service must continue Assuming that arbitration resolves the matter. It resolves the legal question and not the political one Believing the tender price where it is materially below the rest of the field F 78

title: Termination, and who pays for what
blockname: Contracts that do not hold
notes: Termination compensation is where the real risk allocation of a contract becomes visible. A structure that looks like risk transfer often turns out, on reading the termination clauses, to leave the state carrying the debt in every scenario. Week 4 returns to this.
text: Termination, and who pays for what F Delmon, ch. 15.5.1.3 and ch. 24.6. 79 Cause Typical compensation to the private party Rationale Authority default Debt in full, equity return, sometimes lost profit The state caused the loss and lenders will not fund otherwise Contractor default Debt only, often at a discount; equity takes the loss Equity bore the performance risk and failed Voluntary termination by the state Debt in full and equity return, as for authority default The state is buying its way out of a bargain it made Force majeure Debt, and equity contributions without a return Neither side caused it, so the loss is shared Corruption Usually debt only, sometimes nothing A deterrent, and often the hardest to enforce in practice

title: Reading a renegotiation
blockname: Contracts that do not hold
notes: The portfolio point is the most useful thing on the slide. A state with forty concessions is running a repeated game and frequently acts as though each contract were a one-off.
text: Reading a renegotiation When a request arrives, four questions establish what is actually happening. What event is being cited, and was it allocated to a party in the contract. Is the request for more money, more time, a lower obligation, or a longer term, since the last of these is the easiest to grant and the most expensive. What is the alternative to agreeing, and is the state willing to face it. And who else is watching, because a concession granted once establishes what a request is worth in every other contract the state holds. The fourth question is the one governments answer worst. Renegotiation is not a bilateral matter; it is a signal to a market. F 80

title: Block F discussion
blockname: Contracts that do not hold
notes: Question one is the sharpest. If everybody knows renegotiation follows, then the tender selects for political skill rather than operating efficiency.
text: Block F discussion Seminar questions If renegotiation is anticipated by everyone, what is the tender actually selecting for? Would a shorter concession, say ten years rather than thirty, reduce renegotiation? What would it cost? A concessionaire requests a tariff increase citing an exchange rate movement outside its control. On what basis should the state decide, and what should have been in the contract? F 81
